title: ACT Reading — Practice Test 1
summary: A full timed enhanced-ACT Reading test: four original passages (literary narrative, social science, paired humanities passages and natural science with a data table), 36 questions in 40 minutes, with an explanation for every answer.

blocks.text: This is a full-length practice test for the **Reading section of the enhanced ACT**. The real section has **36 questions in 40 minutes**. In the real test, **27 questions are scored** (three passages of 9 questions each) and the other passage is unscored, but you will not know which one, so you must treat every passage as if it counts. **In this practice test, all 36 questions count.**

rows: Humanities — paired passages A and B

items: Sit in a quiet place, put your phone away and keep scrap paper and a pencil ready.
Do the whole section in one sitting. The timer starts when you press Start and the section ends automatically after 40 minutes.
Aim for about 10 minutes per passage: roughly 3–4 minutes to read and map it, then about 6 minutes for its 9 questions.
There is no penalty for wrong answers, so answer every question. If you are stuck, eliminate what you can, guess, mark it and move on.
In the real test the section is timed on its own; when time is up you cannot go back to it. Practise the same way.
The score shown at the end is a **practice percentage**, not an official ACT scaled score.

questions.p:
Passage I — Literary Narrative

LITERARY NARRATIVE: This passage is from an original short story. The narrator remembers a summer he spent at his family's fishing camp on Lake Nasser, in southern Egypt.

[1] I was twelve the year my father finally let me live at the fishing camp, though he did not yet let me fish. The camp was nothing more than three huts of reed matting and tin on a bare shoulder of land south of Aswan, where the desert came down to Lake Nasser and simply stopped. From the doorway of our hut the water stretched so far that on hazy mornings I could not tell where the lake ended and the sky began.

[2] My father, Hassan, went out every evening with his partner, Uncle Mahrous, in a wooden boat whose blue paint the sun had long ago bleached almost white. They laid their nets at dusk and pulled them before dawn. I stayed on shore with my grandfather, who was too old for the boat but not, he insisted, too old to be useful. Our job was the nets. Every afternoon we spread them across the warm stones and searched them, knot by knot, for the tears that the fish and the rocks had made.

[3] I hated the work. It was slow, and slowness at twelve feels like a kind of punishment. My grandfather's fingers moved through the mesh as if they could see on their own, while mine tangled the shuttle and pulled knots that slid apart the moment I let go. "A net is only as strong as its worst knot," he would say, and then he would quietly undo mine and tie them again.

[4] I wanted the boat. I wanted to be the one who came back at sunrise with silver fish sliding in the bottom of the hull. Each evening I watched the blue boat shrink into the dark, its lantern a single yellow point, and I felt that real life was happening somewhere out on the water while I sat on the shore with an old man and a pile of string.

[5] My grandfather had been born in a Nubian village that now lay beneath the lake. He rarely spoke of it, but sometimes, when the water was very still, he would point to a place far out where nothing at all could be seen. "There," he would say. "The palm trees were there." I used to look and see only water, and I wondered how a person could miss something so completely invisible.

[6] Then, near the end of August, Uncle Mahrous fell ill with a fever and went back to town. That evening my father stood in the doorway of the hut, looking at the boat and then at me, for a long time. "Bring the lantern," he said at last.

[7] The lake at night was not what I had imagined. There was no excitement in it, only darkness and a cold that rose from the water and settled in my bones. My father rowed in silence to a bay he knew, and we fed the net over the side, its floats bobbing behind us like small heads. Then we waited. For hours we waited while my father watched the stars, and I discovered that a boat could be even slower than a pile of nets.

[8] Before dawn we began to pull. The net came up heavy and cold, and in the grey light I saw fish caught in it here and there. And then I saw the hole. Near the middle, a section of mesh had split wide open, and the knots around it were loose and clumsy. I knew those knots. They were mine—some of the few I had insisted on finishing myself, waving my grandfather away. Whatever fish had swum into that part of the net had swum straight out again.

[9] My father said nothing. He only lifted the torn section, looked at it, and let it fall back into the boat. His silence was worse than any words he might have used.

[10] When we reached the shore, my grandfather was already sitting on the stones with the shuttle in his lap, as though he had known. I sat down beside him without being asked. That afternoon I tied knots until my fingers ached, and when he tested them, not one slipped.

[11] I am older now than my father was that summer, and I no longer fish. But I still think of my grandfather pointing at the empty water, seeing the palm trees that were no longer there. I understand now that he was not looking at nothing. He was looking at something that had been made carefully and then lost, and he had learned to value whatever is made with care. It took a torn net for me to begin to learn the same thing.
questions.q: Which of the following best describes the passage as a whole?
c: A man explains how his family was forced to leave their village when Lake Nasser was formed.
An adult narrator recalls a childhood experience that changed how he valued slow, careful work.
A boy explains why he decided to become a fisherman like his father.
A narrator compares the dangers of fishing at night with the safety of life on the shore.
questions.e: The story moves from the boy hating net mending (paragraph 3) to tying knots that hold (paragraph 10), and the adult narrator states the lesson in paragraph 11. A is too narrow: the lost village is only the grandfather's memory. C is reversed: the narrator says "I no longer fish."

Passage II — Social Science

SOCIAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about the economics of street markets. The economist and the study described are fictional.

[1] To a visitor, a busy street market can look like chaos. Vendors call out prices, buyers push between tables of tomatoes and plastic sandals, and nothing appears to be organized by anyone. Yet economists who study these markets increasingly argue that the noise hides a remarkably efficient system—one that solves problems that large stores spend a great deal of money trying to solve.

[2] Consider prices. In a supermarket, the price of a kilo of oranges is printed on a label and may stay the same for a week. In a street market, the price can change several times in a single morning. A vendor who sees that her oranges are selling quickly may raise her price a little; a vendor who notices that his are softening in the afternoon heat will lower it before they spoil. Economist Leila Haddad, who spent two years recording prices in one weekly market, calls this "pricing by eyesight." No one calculates a formula, but the result, she argues, is that prices follow supply and demand closely.

[3] Haddad's research also challenges a common assumption: that vendors standing side by side, selling nearly identical goods, must be ruining one another. In the market she studied, eleven vegetable sellers worked within thirty metres of one another. Rather than driving each other out of business, they appeared to benefit from being together. Shoppers came to that corner precisely because they knew they could compare many sellers quickly. Economists call this effect clustering, and it helps explain why shops selling the same kind of goods—gold, fabric, spare car parts—so often gather on a single street.

[4] Clustering does not mean that the vendors simply compete on price, however. Haddad found that the most successful sellers were not always the cheapest. Instead, they were the ones who had built relationships. A regular customer might receive an extra handful of herbs, first choice of the fruit, or the right to pay at the end of the month. In exchange, the vendor gained something a supermarket cannot easily buy: loyalty. Haddad estimates that more than half of the sales she observed were made to customers who bought from the same vendor every week.

[5] These relationships also do the work that contracts and credit cards do in more formal markets. When a buyer takes goods today and promises to pay next week, there is no written agreement, no bank, and no court involved. What makes the system work is reputation. In a market where everyone sees everyone else every week, a buyer who fails to pay or a seller who cheats on weights soon finds that people know. In this sense, Haddad writes, the market is "a small town that meets for six hours."

[6] None of this means that street markets are without problems. Vendors usually have little protection when their goods are damaged or when bad weather keeps customers away. Many earn uneven incomes that make saving difficult. And because their businesses are often unregistered, they may have trouble borrowing money to grow. City governments, meanwhile, often see markets as obstacles to traffic and cleanliness, and some have tried to move them into covered buildings at the edge of town.

[7] Haddad is cautious about such moves. Relocation can solve real problems of crowding and hygiene, she acknowledges, but it can also destroy the very features that make a market succeed. A market moved to a distant building may lose the passing customers who stopped on their way to work, and vendors assigned to fixed stalls may be separated from the neighbours whose presence attracted shoppers in the first place. In one relocation she followed, several vendors returned to their old street within a year, preferring the risk of fines to the loss of their customers.

[8] Her conclusion is not that markets should be left untouched, but that any plan to change them should begin by understanding how they already work. "Planners tend to see a market as a place," she writes. "It is better understood as a network—of prices, of neighbours, of promises. Move the place carelessly, and you may break the network."
questions.q: Which of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

Clustering is the only reason that some street markets succeed while others fail.
questions.e: The passage opens by saying the "noise hides a remarkably efficient system" and then explains prices, clustering and reputation. D is too extreme: "only" ignores the paragraphs on pricing and relationships, and A contradicts Haddad's caution about relocation.

Passage III — Humanities (Paired Passages)

HUMANITIES: Passage A is from an original essay by a restorer of historic buildings. Passage B is from an original essay by an architect. Both writers are fictional.

PASSAGE A — "Read the Building First"

[1] When an old building is damaged, the temptation today is to treat the damage as an opportunity. Architects propose glass roofs over ruined halls, steel stairways beside medieval walls, and concrete wings that "speak to" the old stone. I understand the excitement, but I believe it is usually a mistake. A historic building is not a blank page; it is a document, and our first duty is to read it, not to write on it.

[2] Faithful restoration begins with research. Before a single stone is replaced, the restorer studies old drawings, photographs and the building itself: its tool marks, its earlier repairs, the way its walls have settled. Where original materials survive, they are kept. Where they must be replaced, the new work follows the old methods—lime mortar rather than cement, carved stone rather than cast. The aim is not to make the building look new, but to let it continue to be itself.

[3] Critics say that this approach is dishonest, that a restored wall pretends to be older than it is. But careful restorers keep records of every change, and a trained eye can usually find the new work. More importantly, a visitor who walks through a restored gate is meeting the building its makers intended, not a conversation between those makers and a modern architect who arrived centuries later. Honesty lies in the record, not in a clash of styles.

[4] There is also a practical argument. Modern materials do not always age well beside old ones. Cement, for example, is harder than many traditional mortars and can trap moisture, causing the softer stone around it to crumble. And additions designed to "contrast" with a building may, within a few decades, simply look dated: the fashion of one generation fixed permanently to the achievement of another.

[5] None of this means that old buildings cannot be used. A restored house can become a museum, a school or a library. But the use should fit the building, and not the other way around. A building forced to serve a purpose it was never designed for may be damaged by the very changes that were meant to save it.

PASSAGE B — "Let Old Buildings Grow"

[1] Buildings have never stood still. A mosque gains a new minaret, a palace a new wing; a merchant's house is divided into flats and later joined together again. Each of these changes is part of the building's story, and many are beautiful in their own right. To freeze a building at one chosen moment in its life—usually the moment we find most beautiful—is not to respect its history but to edit it.

[2] For this reason, I believe that when a historic building needs new space or new life, any addition should be clearly modern. A glass entrance hall beside an old stone courtyard does not hide what it is. Visitors can see at once which parts are old and which are new, and the old parts gain dignity from the contrast, as a painting does from a plain frame. A copy, on the other hand, blurs the line, and in a few generations no one may remember which arches are original. Imitation, however skilful, quietly rewrites the record.

[3] I do not mean that anything goes. A good addition is modest in size, respects the height and lines of the old building, and could, if necessary, be removed without harming the original. It must also be built of materials that work safely with the old structure rather than damage it, and it should be designed by people who have studied the old building as closely as any restorer would.

[4] Above all, an addition can keep a building alive. An empty, perfectly restored palace that no one can afford to heat, clean or use will slowly decay again. A palace given a modern wing for a library or a concert hall has a reason to be cared for. The best way to protect an old building, in the end, is to make sure that people still need it. Buildings that are used get repaired; buildings that are only admired are too often forgotten.

c: historic buildings should never be used for any new purpose.
restoration should keep original materials and methods rather than add contrasting modern work.
modern architects do not receive enough training in history.
research is more important than repairing damaged buildings.
questions.e: The author argues for "faithful restoration" that keeps original materials and follows old methods, and calls modern additions "usually a mistake." A is contradicted by paragraph 5, which says restored buildings can become museums, schools or libraries.

Passage IV — Natural Science

NATURAL SCIENCE: This passage is from an original article about how migrating birds find their way. The research team and the data in the table are fictional.

[1] Every autumn, millions of small songbirds leave their breeding grounds and fly thousands of kilometres to places they have never seen. Many travel alone and at night. Young birds on their first migration cannot have learned the route from experience, yet many of them set off in roughly the right direction. How they manage this has puzzled scientists for more than a century.

[2] Part of the answer is that birds seem to use several "compasses." Some species steer by the position of the sun. Night migrants can use the pattern of the stars, which they appear to learn while young by watching how the night sky turns around a fixed point. Landmarks such as coastlines and mountain ranges help too. But one of the most intriguing tools is invisible: Earth's magnetic field.

[3] Earth behaves somewhat like a giant magnet. Its magnetic field lines run between the regions near the poles, and they meet the ground at an angle that changes with location: they are nearly flat near the equator and steeper closer to the poles. In principle, an animal that could sense this angle would know whether it was heading toward the equator or toward a pole, even under a cloudy sky.

[4] Much of the evidence that birds use the field comes from experiments with caged birds. During the migration season, restless birds tend to hop and flutter toward the direction in which they would normally fly. Researchers can surround a cage with electric coils that change the magnetic field inside it and then watch what the birds do. A team led by biologist Hana Okafor recently tested young songbirds of one species this way. Its results are summarized in the table below.

Test condition | Birds tested | Birds facing the normal migration direction
A. Natural magnetic field, dim light | 40 | 33
B. Field turned 90 degrees clockwise, dim light | 40 | 4 (31 others faced 90 degrees clockwise of normal)
C. Field cancelled (almost no field), dim light | 40 | 9
D. Natural magnetic field, complete darkness | 40 | 11

[5] The second result was the most striking. When the coils turned the field by 90 degrees, most of the birds turned with it, as though their inner compass had been rotated. When the field was cancelled, the birds' choices became scattered. Okafor's team concluded that the birds were relying on the magnetic field—not on landmarks or sounds outside the laboratory—to choose a direction.

[6] The last result surprised the team. In complete darkness, with a perfectly normal field, the birds also lost their sense of direction. This fits one of the main ideas scientists have proposed about how the magnetic sense works: that it depends partly on light-sensitive molecules in the bird's eyes. If this idea is correct, a bird might in some way "see" the magnetic field, though no one yet knows what this would look like to the bird. Another proposal is that tiny iron-rich particles somewhere in the body respond to the field like the needle of a compass. The two systems might even work together.

[7] Okafor is careful not to claim too much. Her birds were tested in cages, not in open sky, and only one species was studied. "A bird in a cage is telling us what it would like to do," she notes, "not what it would actually do over a sea at night." Still, experiments like hers suggest that the magnetic sense is not a minor backup but a central part of how many birds find their way. Her team now plans to study other species and to follow birds in the wild.

[8] The research raises new questions as well. If birds rely on such a delicate sense, some scientists wonder whether electrical noise from human sources might sometimes confuse them. That question, like much about this remarkable ability, is still being investigated.
questions.q: The main idea of the passage is that:
c: birds rely only on Earth's magnetic field to migrate.
Earth's magnetic field is one of several cues birds use, and experiments suggest it plays a major role.
scientists now fully understand how birds sense the magnetic field.
electrical noise from human sources is the main danger to migrating birds.
questions.e: Paragraph 2 lists several "compasses," and the rest of the passage presents evidence that the magnetic sense is "a central part" of navigation. A is too extreme ("only"), and C is contradicted by paragraph 6 ("no one yet knows").
